catalog_quote: Greenfield 2012, p. 13: As shown in this study, the phonetic realizations of stops are influenced by stress. In uninflected words, stress is usually final. In inflected words stress is usually penultimate. Most of the forms used in this study have a suffix and all take stress on the penultimate syllable.[15] [fn. 15] Stress in the Katío language is much more complicated than this. It varies in uninflected words, but it mostly falls on the final syllable. When it fails to do so, it is penultimate. A discussion of the factors involved is beyond the scope of this thesis. || Carlson 2015, pp. 70-71: As shown in (120) with ergative ba and topic marker ra, and in (121) with dative á and ra, the presence of these morphemes causes the placement of stress in the prosodic word to be shifted. A trochaic foot is aligned with the right edge of the prosodic word, and the stress pattern shows that these morphemes are included in that domain. When two occur after the same word, such as in (120c) and (121c), it is the first of the two that receives the stress of the trochaic foot. ... Katío appears to prohibit stress preceding the penult, resulting in examples like (120b) and (121b).

new_statements.quote: As shown in this study, the phonetic realizations of stops are influenced by stress. In uninflected words, stress is usually final. In inflected words stress is usually penultimate. Most of the forms used in this study have a suffix and all take stress on the penultimate syllable.[15] [fn. 15:] Stress in the Katío language is much more complicated than this. It varies in uninflected words, but it mostly falls on the final syllable. When it fails to do so, it is penultimate. A discussion of the factors involved is beyond the scope of this thesis.

When it fails to do so, it is penultimate. A discussion of the fa…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is on one of the last two syllables. Greenfield (acoustic study, Córdoba and Antioquia speakers): bare uninflected words mostly take final stress, otherwise penultimate; suffixed words take penultimate stress (e.g. /kʰa.ˈdo/ 'rat', /u.ˈsa/ 'dog', /pʰe.ˈpʰe.na/ 'fan', /kʰewaˈɾa-ta/). Carlson 2015 (pp. 70-71) analyses the same language as a trochaic foot aligned with the right edge of the prosodic word, i.e. penultimate stress over stem + case/topic enclitics ([ˈwũ̯ẽn̆ã] 'woman', [wũ̯ẽˈn̆ãᵐba] 'woman=erg', [wũ̯ẽn̆ãˈᵐbaɾa] 'woman=erg=top'; [damã toro.ˈaɾa]) and states stress never precedes the penult. The two accounts agree on the inflected/cliticised word (penult) but differ on bare words (mostly final vs. penult), and Greenfield says the conditioning factors are unresolved; hence no single fixed position can be assigned yet.
new_statements.exceptions: Greenfield fn. 15: stress 'varies' in uninflected words; final is the majority pattern, penultimate the alternative, factors not discussed. Carlson: when two enclitics follow a host, the first enclitic bears the stress ([toro.ˈaɾa]); stress cannot fall before the penult.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level. Greenfield: isolated words in a carrier sentence, five male speakers from Córdoba (Alto Sinú, 'Koribibida') and Antioquia ('Eyabida'). Carlson: prosodic word = stem plus case/pragmatic enclitics (=ba, =á, =ta, =ra), elicited from consultants from Dabeiba (Antioquia) and Alto San Jorge (Córdoba); phrase 'dama torro' 'white snake' shows stress on the last word only.
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened theses describe Emberá-Catío proper (embe1260, ISO cto): Greenfield's speakers are Katío of Córdoba (Alto Sinú, self-named Koribibida) and of Antioquia (Eyabida); Carlson's consultants are from Dabeiba (Antioquia) and Alto San Jorge (Córdoba). Note that Glottolog 5.3 now separates Northern Emberá [emp] as nort2972 (Darién/Panama, 'Northern Embera Proper'); Mortensen 1999 on the list of works to obtain covers both languoids.

tone_statements.citation: Constenla Umaña, Adolfo & Enrique Margery Peña. 1991. Elementos de fonología comparada chocó. Revista de Filología y Lingüística de la Universidad de Costa Rica 17(1-2): 137-191.
tone_statements.quote: En general, el tono parece ser más importante que la intensidad (véase, por ejemplo, Rex y Schöttelndreyer 1973: 79) en la manifestación fonética del acento y ciertas observaciones de Loewen (1958: 20, nota 4) sugieren incluso la posibilidad de que el sambú sea una lengua tonal [...]. No obstante, por el momento, todos los autores coinciden en asignar a las lenguas la condición de acentuales [...]. En dichas palabras, en los conjuntos de cognados, él acento recae en la penúltima sílaba casi sin excepciones en saija y chamí [...], en tanto que en catío y sambú puede recaer lo mismo en la penúltima que en la última.
tone_statements.translation: In general, pitch seems to be more important than intensity (see, e.g., Rex & Schöttelndreyer 1973: 79) in the phonetic realisation of the accent, and certain observations of Loewen (1958: 20, n. 4) even suggest the possibility that Sambú is a tone language [...]. Nevertheless, for the moment, all authors agree in classing the languages as accentual [...]. In such words, in the cognate sets, the accent falls on the penultimate syllable almost without exception in Saija and Chamí [...], whereas in Catío and Sambú it may fall on the penultimate or on the final syllable alike.

sources.citation: Greenfield Vélez, Gisella Teresa. 2012. The acoustic qualities of Embera Katío stops. MA thesis, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks. §1.3 Phonological Sketch of Embera Katío Stops.
sources.quote: As shown in this study, the phonetic realizations of stops are influenced by stress. In uninflected words, stress is usually final. In inflected words stress is usually penultimate. Most of the forms used in this study have a suffix and all take stress on the penultimate syllable.[15] [fn. 15:] Stress in the Katío language is much more complicated than this. It varies in uninflected words, but it mostly falls on the final syllable. When it fails to do so, it is penultimate. A discussion of the factors involved is beyond the scope of this thesis.
sources.note: §1.3 'Phonological Sketch of Embera Katío Stops', p. 13 + fn. 15: 'In uninflected words, stress is usually final. In inflected words stress is usually penultimate'; footnote: stress 'varies in uninflected words, but it mostly falls on the final syllable. When it fails to do so, it is penultimate'; §4.2.2 (pp. 93-94) measures stress effects (longer closure, shorter FOT in stressed syllables). Speakers: five men from Córdoba (Alto Sinú) and Antioquia.

sources.locator: printed p. 62, §5 'Comparaciones léxicas', points 10-11; comparative 145-item lexicon Dabeiba vs Cristianía with accent marks on pp. 63-66
sources.note: Only statement on accent in the article: most words of the Dabeiba/northern dialect carry final ('agudo') stress, versus penultimate in the south; 47 of 145 compared items differ only in accent. It is a positional tendency read off a comparative wordlist (mostly nouns/roots, accent marked on cited forms), not a rule with conditions; no secondary stress, no weight, no domain, no exceptions stated. The catalog codes stress as 'morphological' with an empty rule; Pardo gives no morphological conditioning, so this adds a default-final-position generalization rather than confirming or contradicting
